mcqs.question: CPU execution time of a program is given by:
options: Execution time = Instruction count × CPI × Clock cycle time
Execution time = Instruction count × Clock rate × CPI
Execution time = Instruction count / (CPI × Clock cycle time)
Execution time = CPI / (Instruction count × Clock cycle time)

mcqs.question: Machine A executes a program of 5 × 10⁹ instructions in 2 seconds. The instruction execution rate of machine A is:
options: 2.5 × 10⁹ instructions per second
4 × 10⁹ instructions per second
1 × 10¹⁰ instructions per second
2.5 × 10⁶ instructions per second

mcqs.question: Machine B executes the same program with 6 × 10⁹ instructions in 1.5 seconds. The instruction execution rate of machine B is:
options: 2.5 × 10⁹ instructions per second
4 × 10⁹ instructions per second
9 × 10⁹ instructions per second
4.5 × 10⁹ instructions per second

mcqs.question: Computer A has a clock cycle time of 250 ps and a CPI of 2.0. Computer B has a clock cycle time of 500 ps and a CPI of 1.2 for the same program. Which computer is faster, and by how much?
options: B is 1.2 times faster than A
A and B are equally fast
A is 1.2 times faster than B
B is 2 times faster than A

mcqs.question: For program 1, machine M1 has an execution time of 2.0 s, a clock rate of 3 × 10⁹ Hz and an instruction count of 5 × 10⁹. The CPI of M1 for this program is:
A program section has an instruction count of 7.5 × 10⁹, a CPI of 1.2 and runs on a machine with a clock rate of 5 × 10⁹ Hz. Its CPU execution time is:
options: 1.8 seconds
0.6 seconds
3.0 seconds
45 seconds

mcqs.question: Speedup obtained from an enhancement is defined as:
options: Execution time with the enhancement / Execution time without the enhancement
Execution time without the enhancement / Execution time with the enhancement
Clock rate with the enhancement / Clock rate without the enhancement
CPI without the enhancement / CPI with the enhancement

options: 216 bits
248 bits
224 bits
320 bits

mcqs.question: For the expression C = A + B, the total code size on an accumulator architecture (Load A = 72, Add B = 72, Store C = 72 bits) is:
options: 216 bits
224 bits
248 bits
320 bits

mcqs.question: For the expression C = A + B, the total code size on a register–register (load-store) architecture, with each instruction of 80 bits and four instructions needed, is:
options: 248 bits
216 bits
224 bits
320 bits

mcqs.question: A disadvantage of the register–register architecture is:
options: Operands are not equivalent, so a source operand is destroyed
Higher instruction count than memory-reference architectures, giving larger programs
A memory bottleneck caused by all operands coming from memory
Large variation in instruction size

mcqs.question: A disadvantage of the memory–memory architecture is:
options: Simple, fixed-length instruction decoding
It wastes registers for temporary storage
Large variation in instruction size and in work per instruction, with a memory bottleneck
Code generation is very complex

Pipelining is best defined as:
options: Executing one instruction completely before starting the next
A technique in which several instructions are overlapped in execution, each at a different processing stage
Executing the same instruction on many data items at once
Predicting the outcome of branches before they execute

mcqs.question: The instruction cycle (fetch–decode–execute cycle) is the process by which a computer:
options: Transfers data between main memory and cache
Compiles a high-level program into machine code
Retrieves an instruction from memory, determines the actions it requires, and carries out those actions
Schedules processes on the CPU

mcqs.question: A single-stage non-pipelined machine has a cycle time of 5 ns. A pipelined version has 5 stages with a cycle time of 1 ns. Assuming no stalls, the speedup of the pipelined machine is:
If the 5-stage pipelined machine stalls 1 cycle for 40% of the instructions, the speedup over the single-stage machine becomes:
The speedup of a pipeline accounting for stalls is given by:
options: Pipeline depth × (1 + stall cycles per instruction)
1 / (Pipeline depth + stall cycles per instruction)
Pipeline depth / (1 + stall cycles per instruction)
(1 + stall cycles per instruction) / Pipeline depth

mcqs.question: For a load instruction, the stage delays are: instruction fetch 150 ps, decode 70 ps, register read 60 ps, ALU 200 ps, memory read 60 ps and register write 150 ps. The clock cycle length of the single-cycle datapath is:
options: 540 ps
690 ps
480 ps
200 ps

mcqs.question: The clock frequency of the single-cycle processor with a 690 ps clock cycle is approximately:
options: 5 GHz
1.45 GHz
0.69 GHz
2.9 GHz

mcqs.question: In a 5-stage pipelined datapath whose slowest stage takes 200 ps, the fastest possible clock cycle and clock frequency are:
options: 690 ps and 1.45 GHz
60 ps and 16.7 GHz
200 ps and 5 GHz
1000 ps and 1 GHz

The purpose of a branch predictor in a pipelined processor is to:
options: Execute both paths of a branch simultaneously
Guess which way a branch will go before it is known for sure, improving the flow of the instruction pipeline
Remove branch instructions from the program
Increase the size of the branch target buffer

mcqs.question: In the static branch prediction scheme used in the ARM11 MPCore processor:
options: All branches are predicted taken
The prediction is based on the branch history table
Forward conditional branches are predicted not taken and backward branches are predicted taken
Branches are never predicted

mcqs.question: Dynamic branch prediction is based on:
options: Caching previously seen branches (e.g. in a BTAC/BTB) and using their past behaviour
The direction of the branch offset only
Compiler hints inserted in the code
Executing the branch at fetch time

mcqs.question: A branch has the outcome pattern T–N–T–N–T–N over one execution of a program core. The accuracy of an 'always taken' predictor for this branch is:

options: It uses no buffer space
A branch must be mispredicted twice in a row before the prediction direction changes, so one unusual outcome does not flip the prediction
It always predicts correctly
It predicts the branch target as well as the direction

mcqs.question: If a branch target buffer (BTB) stores the target instruction of an unconditional branch and there is a BTB hit in instruction fetch, the branch penalty becomes:
options: 2 cycles
0 cycles
−1 cycle (a gain of one cycle)
1 cycle

options: It has no significant effect, because a single predictor serving one branch is generally more accurate, and with a larger buffer two branches are less likely to share one predictor
It doubles the accuracy of both branches
It makes both branches share one predictor
It removes all mispredictions of the two branches

mcqs.question: The key difference between a branch instruction and a jump instruction is:
options: Branches are unconditional while jumps are conditional
Jumps modify the program counter to a specified address, while branches are relative to the current program counter and may be conditional
Branches change the program counter while jumps do not
There is no difference

mcqs.question: An anti-dependence (WAR) exists between two instructions when:
options: The first instruction writes a location that the second reads
An instruction reads a register or memory location and a subsequent instruction writes a new value to the same location
Both instructions write the same location
Both instructions read the same location

mcqs.question: In the code: ADD R3, R1, R2 / SW R3, 12(R0) / LW R4, 0(R0) / ADD R5, R1, R4 — the true (RAW) dependences are:
options: SW depends on LW through R0
ADD R3 → SW through R3, and LW → ADD R5 through R4
ADD R5 depends on ADD R3 through R1
There are no dependences

mcqs.question: An array index is called affine if it can be written in the form:
options: a × i + b, where a and b are constants and i is the loop index
i² + b
a × i × j, with two loop indices
Any expression involving an array name

mcqs.question: In the GCD dependence test for two affine references a·i + b and c·i + d, a dependence may exist only if:
options: GCD(a, c) divides (d − b)
a equals c
(d − b) is greater than GCD(a, c)
The loop is first normalised

mcqs.question: Static scheduling differs from dynamic scheduling in that:
options: Static scheduling is done by the hardware at run time
In static scheduling the compiler arranges instructions to avoid stalls, while in dynamic scheduling the hardware decides the order of execution at run time
Dynamic scheduling is done by the compiler before execution
Static scheduling allows instructions to execute out of order

mcqs.question: With dynamic scheduling, when an instruction stalls:
options: All following instructions must also stop
The whole pipeline is flushed
Following instructions can still issue if they create no structural hazards or dependences
The compiler reschedules the code

mcqs.question: An exception is called precise if:
options: It is detected in the same cycle in which it occurs
The machine state is exactly as if the instructions had executed sequentially, with all instructions before the excepting one completed and none after it having taken effect
It never occurs during multiply and divide instructions
It is handled entirely by software

mcqs.question: A finite state machine (FSM) is:
options: A machine with an infinite number of states
An abstract machine that can be in exactly one of a finite number of states at any time
A type of cache memory
A scheduling algorithm for processes

mcqs.question: In SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) multimedia operations, a partitioned add on 16-bit data within a 64-bit ALU performs:
options: One 64-bit addition
Two 32-bit additions only
Four 16-bit additions in a single clock cycle, with carries between the partitions prevented
Sixteen 4-bit additions

mcqs.question: A pixel in graphics processing is typically 32 bits, consisting of:
options: Two 16-bit channels
Four 8-bit channels: R (red), G (green), B (blue) and A (attribute/transparency)
One 32-bit floating-point value
Eight 4-bit channels

mcqs.question: In MIPS floating-point instructions, MOV.S and MOV.D respectively copy:
options: A single-precision register and a double-precision register to another register of the same type
Memory to a register and a register to memory
An integer register and a floating-point register
Two single-precision registers at the same time

mcqs.question: A vertex, a common 3D data type in graphics applications, consists of:
options: A single 64-bit integer
Four components (x, y, z) and w, usually 32-bit floating-point values
Four 8-bit colour channels
Two components (x, y) only
